meta.what: Open walls (blockers) and the accepted-risk record: known ways the work can still go wrong, where a fix exists and has not been paid for, each with who decided.

blocker_states.in progress: narrowed, or a fix is being built
blocker_states.not started: open, with no fix under way

decisions.accepted by the owner: the project owner accepted the risk, often as interim
decisions.bug-for-bug compatible with Apple: the owner accepted it because it is what Apple's own system does, on the hardware macOS 27 ships on (the term is Wine's: it aims at "bug-for-bug" compatibility with Windows); a stricter choice was possible and was declined, and the record is looked at again if Apple changes. Never used where the project is looser than Apple
decisions.direction set by the owner: not accepted as a gap; the owner chose the fix
decisions.project default: fails loudly and loses nothing, so the project accepted it by its own rule; the owner may overturn it
decisions.pending the owner: could fail silently or loosens a policy, so only the owner may accept it; not yet decided
decisions.fixed: the fix was built and measured
decisions.retired: the thing it was about is no longer used day to day

meta.how_gaps_are_judged: Every gap is judged by three questions: what the fix costs, whether the gap arises on the macOS 27 path at all, and whether a general translation route would close it along with others. The project's rule is also to compare how Rosetta, Wine, QEMU, FEX-Emu and box64 handle the same thing, and to copy them where they agree. Most records carry such a comparison, but not all: some were judged not to be translation gaps (a value the boot loader supplies, a limit of the project's own test script), at least one still owes its comparison until its cause is read, one has no comparison field at all, and at least one says outright that no translator was compared. The comparisons are in the project's private working notes, not in this table. Where the project's behaviour equals Apple's own, on the hardware macOS 27 ships on, and being stricter would be optional, the project matches Apple rather than being stricter, and records the case as bug-for-bug compatible with Apple.
meta.selection: The risks table is a selection: 52 rows drawn from the project's register of 83 accepted-risk records. Related records are combined into one row (for example, eight path-rewriting corner cases are one row). Which records were left out, and why, is not recorded here. The register's total is the last snapshot's 82 plus the one record added since (G-52's); counts of the register's ID fields differ from it by one or two, depending on how combined records are counted.

blockers.title: Identity of a program under translation
blockers.note: The kernel's exec option gives an arm64e program its own Apple identity. For a recompiled program that must be a platform binary, a lab key is trusted through Apple's developer trusted-key mechanism; how that would work in a user install is undecided.

blockers.title: No Data volume beside 27's system volume
blockers.note: The volume group id was written offline; a real volume group boots.

blockers.title: Mounting the Preboot volume needs an arm64e-only program
blockers.note: Closed by a 945-byte stand-in script; lifting 27's mount would retire it.

blockers.title: No x86_64 Sandbox kext for 27
blockers.note: 27's own Sandbox kext, recompiled, boots and enforces. Inside it: network-outbound rows are no reading, a sysctl deny is not closed, and ten deny pairs against real 27 are undecided.

blockers.title: fork safety under translation
blockers.note: 15,500 children at 4 vCPU: none hung, none wrong, no guest panic; the 1,000 that died did so where the native program dies the same way. 8 vCPU under heavy host load not retested.

blockers.title: pid 1 from 27's own launchd
blockers.note: Works on the furthest configuration (3 boots); since 2026-11-24 also in the default test base, one standalone disk image (2 test boots). Whether the lab trusted-key route stays is the owner's decision.

blockers.title: Display-state mismatch and the backdrop abort (hybrid image)
blockers.note: Both are small byte edits on disk, found by pattern per build. One risk, that an edit could be silently wrong, is the owner's to accept.

blockers.title: No GPU
blockers.note: Below the main line. A software Vulkan compute test passes in the guest.

blockers.title: Building the kernel collection with 27's own tools
blockers.note: Still macOS 26's kmutil in a recovery guest. 27's kmutil runs under translation but has not loaded a kext.

blockers.title: 27's own logd
blockers.note: 27's own logd and logd_helper run translated on the furthest configuration, exit status 0 in 3 of 3 boots. Reading messages back through 27's logd is measured only on other configurations (2 of 2), not yet on this one.

blockers.title: 27's own amfid
blockers.note: Runs and stays up (4 boots). In one boot it refused an ad hoc signed program carrying a restricted entitlement; an edited-signature test did not discriminate, so validation is partly tested. A recompiled amfid has not been linked with the current tools.

blockers.title: Daemons that run but do not yet serve
blockers.note: In one boot, before 27's own amfid replaced macOS 26's, 126 of the 411 labels in launchd's job table ran and 15 had a nonzero status; causes of 12 of them are unread.

blockers.title: DEVELOPMENT build of the self-built kernel
blockers.note: Boots; core daemons end themselves in a loop.

blockers.title: A circular wait at exec that could freeze the boot
blockers.note: Read from kernel stacks in five boots; removed in kernel 1.4.3, with a follow-up fix in 1.4.4.

blockers.title: The first translated run of a boot is slow
blockers.note: Up to 233 s and 412 s for a first read, 9 to 65 s later, on a host at load 130 to 198 with no translation cache kept across boots. Not split between translation cost and starvation.

blockers.title: File flags lost on the Data volume
blockers.note: Restored and read back, 14,024 of 14,024 flagged entries equal.

blockers.title: 27's sandboxd staying up under launchd is not shown
blockers.note: Traced to a refused write to guest memory; a translator fix removed it for a hand-started copy in 2 of 2 boots, while in the second the launchd-started copy kept restarting (with a trace option the hand-started one lacked). That fix (patch X) had an open race and has been replaced by patch Y, whose boots are not written up in this record yet.

blockers.title: The 240-second registry stall and the HID driver extension
blockers.note: An arm64e-only DriverKit serial extension, whose kernel side (com.apple.driver.driverkit.serial) had no x86_64 build in the boot collection, keeps IOUserResources from ever matching (the mechanism is inference; the fixes are measured). Two fixes work: Apple's x86_64 IOUserSerial.kext from the Kernel Debug Kit added to the boot collection (4 boots), or the extension moved out of the scanned folder (7 boots). With either, the registry went quiet in every boot, and no stall line or hidden disk was seen in any boot that counted them. With the registry quiet, 27's own DiskArbitration served the scratch-disk round in 7 of 8 boots counted. The project's default test base, adopted on 2026-11-24, carries the first fix (2 test boots); most rows of this record predate that base. The HID extension's crash at start is fixed in 3 boots (docs/boot-programs.md). Keyboard input typed at the login window has reached it in each login boot since (B21); pointer events reached the HID queue in earlier boots, but whether a click reaches a control is not tested. Both written up for other projects: docs/notes-for-liberator.md.

blockers.title: A launchd-managed sshd on the furthest configuration
blockers.note: Logins so far are to a debug sshd the test payload starts.

blockers.title: Stopping a service panicked the guest
blockers.note: The recompiled launchd exited when it stopped a service, and the kernel panicked (1 control boot). With the fix: 0 panics in 2 boots; in one, launchd waited its 10 s exit timeout, then killed a service that ignored the stop request, and stayed pid 1.

blockers.title: No login window on the display test overlays
blockers.note: Closed: the login window appears. In the six boots this row first counted, WindowServer stayed up and in 5 of them showed the boot progress window (the sixth stayed on the text console), but no login window appeared. Whether it appears looks like a race: SecurityAgent has to show its window before the guest's display goes to sleep, and once the display sleeps nothing redraws it (inferred from one boot's timing, in which SecurityAgent logged that it was showing its window one second before the screens slept). The window was drawn in 2 of 2 boots of one set-up and 1 of 2 of another when nothing held the display awake, and in each of 7 later boots in which a login was typed. In 4 other boots, set up differently, it did not appear; the cause is read for some of them only. Two more boots on 2026-11-24, set up differently again, showed none either (B22). What follows the login: B22.

blockers.title: No desktop after the first login
blockers.note: After the first login, User Account Updater completes (2 boots), then loginwindow launches the first-login Setup Assistant. In the first boot it became the frontmost app, but no pane of it appeared; the screen stayed black to the end of the boot, and no Dock or Finder process started, and the disk also ran out of space about a minute after Setup Assistant was launched (B23). A second boot that reached it, on 2026-11-24, ended the same way (the same final frame, byte for byte; Dock, Finder and SystemUIServer never started), and the disk did not run out (lowest free space about 2.15 GiB), so running out of space is not why (1 boot). In that boot Setup Assistant's record for the user had been marked complete beforehand; the first-login updater logged that the account was a new user account and wrote the record back, and Setup Assistant was launched anyway. Why no pane appears is not read; that it is Setup Assistant's own fault rather than drawing or compositing is not shown. Boots that did not reach a login window: a try with that record marked complete (1 boot; cause not read); a clean root with that record and B23's fix used by nearly every translated program (1 boot; the guest's load rose past 300 with many translated programs waiting to run; why is inferred, not shown); and a boot with a per-user marker that may let the first login skip Setup Assistant (whether it does is not read), and a later build of B23's fix named for those 81 programs and 16 more of the login session (1 boot; the guest was not overloaded, its load falling to 7; cause not read). A control boot for the last, with the earlier build, has no result yet.

blockers.title: The translator's shared-cache data fills the disk
blockers.note: The translator's store of slid shared-cache data (docs/translator-patches.md, R) is kept per home directory, and macOS gives every sandbox container and daemon user its own, so the same files are copied into a store for each that uses it: in one boot 16 stores held about 9 GiB of cache files, mostly duplicated slid data, and the root's 51.5 GB container ran out of space. A fix keeps one root-owned store for every user (R2): built, its cache tests pass, and a later build of it passed the whole test suite. The first build has booted in two arrangements on 2026-11-24 (1 boot each). With nearly every translated program on it, the shared store held one copy (14 data files, about 560 MiB) and the disk did not fill, but no login window appeared. Named for 81 programs on the login path, with another build as the default, the login went through, but the programs on the other build made 140 copies in 10 per-home stores, and free space fell to about 2.15 GiB by the end of the boot. So disk use through a login with every program on the fix is not shown yet. The later build has booted once, with no login window (B22). That every user's processes trust root's copy is a lab policy the owner has not ruled on.

risks.risk: With the exec option on, a native process may register a signature form Apple's Intel kernel would refuse
risks.note: Matches Apple's kernel on Apple silicon, where macOS 27 ships: from Apple's published source, it accepts code-signature pages of 4 KiB or of the kernel's own page size, from every process. On Apple silicon that page is 16 KiB, which is the page size a native process reads there; the source does not fix it. Apple's Intel kernel accepts 4 KiB only, so the match is with the Apple silicon kernel, not the Intel one. A stricter kernel was built and not adopted: it would refuse a registration one of Apple's own drivers makes on every boot checked (four). Nothing wrong measured.

risks.risk: Every way programs run here needs Apple's x86_64 libraries, which macOS 27 ships for Rosetta and a later release may drop
risks.note: Native and recompiled programs load them; the translator itself starts on Apple's x86_64 dyld and libSystem. macOS 27, the target, ships them. Apple has said general-purpose Rosetta stays through macOS 27 and only a subset after. A translator needing no x86_64 user space would remove most of the exposure; it is not started (docs/roadmap.md).
